title: Sharing and Taking Turns: Yours, Mine, Ours

body.heading: Three kinds of things
paragraphs: Grown-ups say 'share!' a lot, but sharing has rules that make it fair. Everything around you belongs in one of three groups.
Knowing the groups stops most sharing fights before they start.

body.heading: Yours, everyone's, turns
paragraphs: YOURS — A few special things are only yours: your lovey, your birthday gift, the picture you just drew. You may say, 'This is special to me. Please don't take it.' That is allowed.
EVERYONE'S — Some things belong to everyone: the park swing, the classroom blocks, the library books. Nobody owns them, so everybody shares them.
TURNS — For everyone's-things that only one person can use at a time, we take turns. A turn has a start and an end — a timer, a song, or counting to twenty can mark the end fairly.

body.heading: How to ask, how to wait
paragraphs: Ask with words: 'When you are finished, may I have a turn?' Asking works better than grabbing — grabbing starts fights and loses turns.
Waiting is the hard part. While you wait, watch, plan your turn, or find a for-now toy. Waiting well is a skill, and it grows like a muscle.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Sort five of your toys into the three groups: yours, everyone's, turns. Is there one you would move to a different group?
2. What could mark the end of a turn at your house — a timer, a song, or counting? Pick one together.

takeaway: Sharing is fair when we know the groups — special things are yours, shared things are everyone's, and a clear end (timer, song, count) makes turns work.
